title: When to Use Microservices
description: Learn to identify scenarios where microservices provide the most value and when to avoid them.

data.text: Choosing the right architecture is about context. Google, Amazon, and Netflix did not start with microservices; they evolved into them as their user bases and engineering teams grew. Understanding when to adopt microservices is just as important as knowing how to build them.

data.title: Strong Indicators for Microservices
items: Your engineering team is large enough that coordination overhead is slowing delivery
Different parts of your application have very different scaling requirements
You need to deploy parts of your system independently multiple times per day
You want to experiment with different technologies for different components
Your monolith has become difficult to maintain and change

data.title: Avoid Microservices When
items: Your team is smaller than 10-15 engineers
You are building an MVP or proof of concept
Your application has simple, well-understood domain boundaries
You lack the operational expertise to manage distributed systems
Performance and latency are critical and network overhead would hurt

data.title: The Strangler Fig Pattern
data.text: If you are unsure, start with a monolith and use the Strangler Fig pattern to incrementally extract services. This lets you gain microservices experience without a big-bang rewrite.

data.title: Example: E-commerce Platform Decision
data.content: A startup building an e-commerce site with 3 engineers should start with a monolith. Once the team grows to 20+ engineers and the payment, inventory, and recommendation systems need independent scaling, microservices become appropriate.
data.code:
# Monolith-first approach
# Initially, everything in one deployable unit:
# - User management
# - Product catalog
# - Shopping cart
# - Order processing
# - Payment integration

# Later, extract services one by one:
# Step 1: Extract payments (most independent scaling need)
# Step 2: Extract product catalog (read-heavy, caching opportunity)
# Step 3: Extract recommendations (ML/AI heavy workload)

data.caption: Decision flow for microservices adoption

items.question: What if I choose wrong?
items.answer: You can migrate. Many companies moved from monoliths to microservices (Netflix, Amazon) and some have moved back to a modular monolith for simplicity.

items.question: Does industry size matter?
items.answer: Yes. Startups usually start with monoliths; large enterprises often use microservices because they have the teams and operational maturity to support them.

items.question: What about serverless?
items.answer: Serverless can complement microservices. Use microservices for core domains and serverless functions for event-driven or sporadic workloads.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Start with a monolith unless you have a clear reason not to
Microservices solve team coordination and scaling problems
The Strangler Fig pattern lets you evolve safely
Reevaluate your architecture as your team and product grow
data.takeaway: Choose the simplest architecture that meets your current needs; evolve it as requirements change.
